Here is what happened in AI today. Each item links to the full story, with plain-language explanations of anything unfamiliar. The links go to a website built especially for you, with a new edition every day, so do check it out.

Question of the day: How do old Soviet cartoons get their sharpness back? The film has been lying in an archive for half a century, yet on the screen Mowgli suddenly looks as if he was drawn yesterday. The answer is at the end of this email.

  • The Riemann hypothesis proof found with Claude is correct, say the people who maintain the proof-checking program. The proof of the Riemann hypothesis that Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge found with Claude is correct, according to a joint statement by the communities that maintain Lean, the program used to check it. Dozens of people ran the 17 million lines of code, independent tools confirmed it proves the real hypothesis and not a look-alike, and several separately written checking programs accepted it. What is still missing is understanding: no human has yet read the argument through or can explain why it works. Anthropic makes Claude, the AI writing this digest. Read more and the background.
  • METR, an independent tester: AI is improving at research work so fast that it is getting hard to measure. METR, a non-profit that tests AI from the outside, says public AI models now usually match or beat skilled people on clearly defined programming tasks, and that the length of task they can complete is doubling about every 3.6 months. It says the public evidence can no longer rule out a drastic speed-up in AI research within a couple of years, so fast that people could not keep track of the risks. It also finds models still show worse judgment than experts where there is no quick feedback, and warns that today’s tests may flatter them. Read more and the background.
  • UN talks on “killer robots” end with an agreement to keep talking for two more years. A week of United Nations talks in Geneva on “killer robots”, weapons that choose and strike targets without a human decision, ended without binding rules. Countries agreed only to work on a possible accord by 2028. Seven countries had wanted real negotiations to begin; campaigners blame Russia above all, and also the United States, for blocking stronger wording. Every decision there needs the agreement of all 128 member countries. Read more and the background.
  • Meta’s emissions jump by about 40% in a year, and it puts its 2030 climate promise under review. Meta, the owner of Facebook and WhatsApp, says it is “re-evaluating” its promise to reach net-zero emissions by 2030, because demand for AI has grown faster than expected. Its total greenhouse-gas emissions rose nearly 40% in a single year as it built data centres, a bigger jump than at Microsoft, Google or Amazon, none of which has yet backed away from its targets. The figures are Meta’s own, from its yearly report. Read more and the background.

Also on the website today: Put into a simulated office, the best AI programmers finish fewer than one job in twelve, OpenAI’s newest models answer more briefly, and admit doubt less often, a testing firm finds, Trump says he will penalise American companies that build AI data centres abroad; there is no plan yet, After the planted-traps study, a big AI middleman drops three providers.

Answer to the question of the day. An article in the Russian magazine Sistemny Blok explains that the main trouble with old cartoons is usually not scratches or faded colours but low resolution: the video copy simply has too few dots for a modern screen. The studio Soyuzmultfilm restored some films by hand, which is slow. In 2018 Yandex tried a neural network it calls DeepHD, a kind of technology known as “super-resolution”. It works in two steps, each with its own network: the first removes noise and the blocky marks left by video compression, the second enlarges the picture and draws in fine detail. To teach it, engineers took sharp pictures, shrank them, and asked the network to rebuild the originals. A second network acted as an examiner, trying to tell the rebuilt frame from the real one; when it could no longer tell, the first network was doing its job. People on a crowd-work service also voted on which results looked best. In May 2018 the method was tried on classic films such as “The Cranes Are Flying” and “Ivan’s Childhood”, and that autumn on ten Soyuzmultfilm cartoons, among them “The Scarlet Flower”, “The Golden Antelope”, “Thumbelina”, “The Bremen Town Musicians”, the “Mowgli” series and “A Kitten Named Woof”. Backgrounds and characters became crisper. One thing to keep in mind: the network does not recover what the artists drew, it makes a good guess at missing detail. The article, from January 2021, adds that hobbyists can do something similar by hand with ordinary video-editing programs; it just takes far longer. Sistemny Blok, “The return of the sharp parrot: how a neural network restores old Soviet cartoons” (January 2021) (article in Russian).
